read.glossary.0.word.note: "belonging" uses the key term "rasa memiliki". In places where "belong" is a verb I wrote "merasa menjadi bagian dari (kelompok)", since "rasa memiliki" can also mean a sense of ownership.

read.sections.0.text.note: Ubuntu saying "a person is a person through other people" rendered literally as "seseorang menjadi manusia melalui orang lain". The popular Indonesian version is "aku ada karena kita ada" (I am because we are), which is a different English wording.
read.sections.0.text.back: A sense of belonging is the feeling of being accepted and connected to a group. Someone can sit in one room with a group but still feel ignored or not invited. People can be part of many groups at once, such as a class, a sports team, a group of friends, or a club. The group can also be people who use the same language or have the same hobby. Many cultures value connections like this. In southern Africa, people often talk about Ubuntu. Ubuntu is usually explained as "a person becomes human through other people". It means we grow as humans through our connections with other people.
read.sections.0.text.source: Belonging is the feeling of being accepted and connected to a group. A person can sit in a room with a group and still feel ignored or left out. People can belong to many kinds of groups at once, such as a class, a sports team, a group of friends or a club. It might also be people who share a language or a hobby. Many cultures value these connections. In southern Africa, people often talk about Ubuntu. It is usually explained as “a person is a person through other people”. It means we grow as people through our relationships with others.

read.sections.2.text.note: "have a real say" rendered as "benar-benar ikut menentukan" throughout (also in the checks, write and watch). Check it sounds natural.
read.sections.2.text.back: Belonging also grows when people really help decide. One card says: "I want to help choose the activities, not just come". A student planning group makes members more empowered, meaning they have the power to choose and act. The UN agreement on children's rights says children have the right to give their opinion about things that affect them. The agreement also says children may join groups or form groups. A good group asks its members what is going well and what isn't. No one has to tell personal things about their life in order to be part of the group.
read.sections.2.text.source: Belonging also grows when people have a real say. One card says: “I want to help choose the activities, not only attend them”. A student planning group gives members more agency, which means the power to make choices and act. The UN agreement on children's rights says children have the right to give their opinions on things that affect them. It also says they can join or set up groups. A good group asks members what is working and what is not. Nobody should have to share private things about their life to belong.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: A sense of belonging means you feel accepted in a group. You feel close to the people in it. Someone can be in the room but still feel not invited. People can join many groups. For example a class, a team, or friends. It can also be people who use the same language or have the same hobby. In southern Africa, people talk about Ubuntu. It means we grow as humans through other people.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Belonging means you feel accepted in a group. You feel connected to the people in it. A person can be in a room and still feel left out. People can belong to many groups. It can be a class, a team or friends. It can be people who share a language or a hobby. In southern Africa, people talk about Ubuntu. It means we grow as people through other people.

read.sections.1.text.back: A barrier is something that makes it harder for someone to take part. Look at the feedback cards from the youth club. One member finds meetings hard when everyone talks at the same time. Another member only joined after someone explained the rules calmly. The club doesn't need to change its members. Instead, the club can change how it works. A rule of taking turns to speak makes meetings easier to follow, because only one person speaks at a time. A welcome buddy can explain the club's routine to new members. These changes remove barriers, so more people can take part.
read.sections.1.text.source: A barrier is something that makes it harder for someone to take part. Look at the youth club's feedback cards. One member finds meetings difficult when everyone speaks at once. Another member only joined after someone explained the rules quietly. The club does not need to change its members. Instead, it can change how it works. Turn-taking rules make meetings easier to follow, because only one person speaks at a time. A welcome partner can explain the club's routines to new members. These changes remove barriers, so more people can participate.

watch.summary.back: In this video, young people talk about identity, belonging, and feeling empowered in the place where they learn. Their identity grows from their experiences. For example, goals they managed to reach and mistakes they turned into lessons. Belonging grows when adults know the students' names. Belonging also grows when students can share their work without being judged. For them, being empowered means being sure you can reach a goal if you try. Older mentors, friends, and chances to lead can help. At the end of the video, they tell adults that young people are ready to help shape their own lives and schools. The speakers share their own stories, but you don't need to share yours. You can think about these questions with the youth club example, or a group you know.
watch.summary.source: In this video, young people talk about identity, belonging and agency in the places where they learn. Their identity grows from their experiences. These include goals they reached and mistakes they learned from. Belonging grows when adults know students' names. It also grows when students can share their work and not be judged. For them, agency means feeling sure that you can reach a goal if you work at it. Older helpers, friends and chances to lead can help. At the end, they tell adults that young people are ready to help shape their own lives and schools. The speakers share their own stories, but you do not need to share yours. You can think about the questions using the youth club, or a group you know.
